title: Photosynthesis
text:
Okay, good morning everyone, let's get started. Before we begin, a quick reminder that the lab reports are due on Friday, and please put your names on the first page this time, because last week I had three reports with no names at all. Right. So today we are talking about photosynthesis, which is probably the most important chemical process on the planet, and by the end of this hour I want you to be able to explain where the food on your plate really comes from.

Let me start with a story. In the 1600s a Flemish scientist called Jan van Helmont planted a small willow tree in a pot of carefully weighed soil. He watered it for five years. At the end the tree had gained about seventy-four kilograms, but the soil had lost only a few grams. He concluded that the tree was made of water. He was partly wrong, and the missing piece is what we study today.

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. The overall equation is six molecules of carbon dioxide plus six molecules of water, with light energy, giving one molecule of glucose and six molecules of oxygen. So most of the mass of van Helmont's tree actually came from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil and not only from the water.

Where does this happen? Inside the leaf cells there are small green structures called chloroplasts. Chloroplasts contain a green pigment called chlorophyll, and chlorophyll is what absorbs the light. It absorbs red and blue light very well, but it reflects green light, which is exactly why leaves look green to us. My daughter asked me this once and I told her the plant does not want the green light, so it throws it back at us. That is roughly right.

Photosynthesis happens in two stages. The first stage is the light-dependent reactions, which take place in the thylakoid membranes inside the chloroplast. Here light energy splits water molecules, which releases oxygen as a by-product, and the energy is stored in two carrier molecules, ATP and NADPH. So the oxygen you are breathing right now came from split water molecules, not from carbon dioxide. This is a classic exam question and many students get it wrong, so write it down.

The second stage is the Calvin cycle, also called the light-independent reactions, which takes place in the stroma, the fluid around the thylakoids. In the Calvin cycle the plant uses the ATP and NADPH from the first stage to fix carbon dioxide from the air and build it into glucose. The key enzyme here is called RuBisCO, and it is probably the most abundant protein on Earth. It is also surprisingly slow, which is one reason plants need so much of it.

Several factors affect the rate of photosynthesis. Light intensity matters, because more light means more energy for the light reactions, up to a point. Carbon dioxide concentration matters, because the Calvin cycle needs carbon dioxide to make glucose. And temperature matters, because the enzymes work best within a certain range, and above that range they slow down and can be damaged. Farmers use this in greenhouses by adding extra carbon dioxide and keeping the temperature steady to grow tomatoes faster.

Why should you care? Because almost every food chain on Earth starts with photosynthesis. The glucose plants make is used for energy and to build cellulose and starch, and animals, including us, eat the plants or eat animals that ate the plants. Photosynthesis also produces the oxygen in our atmosphere and removes carbon dioxide, which links it directly to climate change.

Okay, that is a lot. Next week we will do respiration, which is basically photosynthesis running backwards. Don't forget the lab reports.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis uses light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
It happens in chloroplasts, where chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green light.
The light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membranes split water, releasing oxygen and making ATP and NADPH.
The Calvin cycle in the stroma uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into glucose with the enzyme RuBisCO.
Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature affect the rate of photosynthesis.
Almost every food chain starts with photosynthesis, which also produces atmospheric oxygen.
